design_detail: Placebo-controlled within-person ketamine challenge in nine people with schizophrenia, described by the authors as double-blind. Each participant received, on four separate days spread over two weeks, three doses of ketamine (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg) and one placebo, each injected intravenously over 60 seconds (pp. 11-12). The order of dose and placebo was chosen by the non-blind staff on safety grounds rather than randomized, and the highest dose was routinely not given first; eleven different orders were used across the fifteen series (nine on haloperidol, six off) (p. 11). All participants were inpatients stabilized on haloperidol 0.3 mg/kg/day for four weeks before the first challenge (on-HAL). Six of the nine were then withdrawn from haloperidol in a separate blinded, placebo-controlled withdrawal and were challenged again after at least four weeks drug-free (off-HAL) (p. 11). Mental status was rated at baseline and 20, 90 and 180 minutes after each injection, and a blind follow-up interview was held at 8 and 24 hours (pp. 11-12).
can_establish: That in nine people with schizophrenia stabilized on haloperidol, a single intravenous bolus of ketamine at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg raised BPRS total and positive-symptom scores 20 minutes later compared with placebo in the same people, that the scores were back at baseline by 90 minutes, and what the induced symptoms looked like clinically.
cannot_establish: Whether haloperidol modifies the effect (the off-haloperidol series has six people, five at the top dose, and its null result is an absence of evidence); any effect on negative symptoms (SANS data were collected but never reported, and Table 2 holds no negative-symptom measure); the shape of the dose-response curve (three doses, no randomized order, p-values only); the frequency or nature of delayed effects (recorded by unsystematic clinical report after the fact); whether people without schizophrenia respond in the same way (no comparison group); and anything about repeated or non-medical use outside a laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Inpatient volunteers on a clinical research ward (Maryland Psychiatric Research Center); participants and their families were informed about the protocol, including the risk of worsening psychosis, and gave consent. The institutional review board restricted the number who could be recruited to the minimum needed to answer the question (p. 10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Diagnosis of schizophrenia by DSM-III-R criteria made by two experienced clinicians from all historical and direct assessment information; actively psychotic but stable; medically healthy by history, examination and laboratory tests; the paper states none had a recent history of drug or alcohol problems (p. 10). Each participant was characterized with the SCID, the Schedule for the Deficit Syndrome, the MPRC Involuntary Movement Scale, the Neurological Evaluation Scale, the Cannon-Spoor Premorbid Adjustment Scale and the Prognostic Scale (p. 10).
sample.demographics: Five men and four women; mean age 30 (SD 9.3), range 22-53; mean length of illness 9.3 years (SD 6.2), range 3-24 (p. 10; Table 1, p. 11). Table 1 gives sex, race, age, illness duration, diagnostic subtype (six paranoid, one disorganized, two undifferentiated), primary negative symptoms, and baseline BPRS thought-disorder and hallucination/delusion item scores for each of the nine.
sample.attrition: All nine completed the on-haloperidol series, but two did not receive the 0.5 mg/kg condition in it (Table 2 gives n=7). Across the whole study three people failed to receive that condition (p. 11): two were withheld for safety by the non-blind observer and given placebo as a blinded substitution, and one had an unrelated infection. Three of the nine did not enter the off-haloperidol series: one was discharged for reasons unrelated to the protocol and two refused the repeat procedure because they had disliked their first ketamine experience; one of those two had had a mild response and the other a large response at all three doses (p. 11). Within the off-haloperidol series, 5 of the 6 received 0.5 mg/kg (Table 4, p. 15).
sample.selection_effects: Nine people, chosen as able to consent and clinically stable enough for a psychotomimetic challenge on a research ward, and small by design because the ethics board capped recruitment. Refusal of the second series by two participants who disliked the first is related to the outcome being measured, so the six retested off haloperidol are not a random subset. The one participant whose symptoms did not change at all was the oldest (53) and had the longest illness (24 years) (p. 12).

exposure.measurement: Ketamine given and measured in the laboratory; no blood concentrations were measured and the preparation (racemic or single enantiomer) is not stated. Participants' own prior drug use was assessed by clinical history only.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: ketamine 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, each injected intravenously over 60 seconds, and one placebo injection, one condition per day on four days spread over two weeks; haloperidol 0.3 mg/kg/day for four weeks before the first series (pp. 11-12). An indwelling forearm catheter was placed one hour before injection; heart rhythm was monitored for 30 minutes after the injection, and pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation were followed (p. 11). No cardiovascular or physiological results are reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Haloperidol was the comparison condition rather than a confounder: the whole first series was run on a fixed dose of it, and the second series after at least four weeks without it. Other psychotropic medication is not mentioned; the paper states no recent history of drug or alcohol problems (p. 10). An extensive milieu, rehabilitation and psychosocial programme ran throughout the admission (p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to the ketamine conditions (all participants were drug-naive to ketamine for the purposes of the study and inpatient throughout). For the off-haloperidol series, at least four weeks neuroleptic-free; the withdrawal was blinded and placebo-controlled and its drug-free period is given as four to eight weeks (p. 11).

comparison.controls: Each participant is his or her own control: a blinded placebo injection in the same four-session series, and, for six of the nine, the same four conditions repeated off haloperidol. There is no group of people without schizophrenia.
comparison.matching: Within-person design. Order was not randomized: the non-blind staff chose it on safety grounds and the highest dose was routinely not given first, so dose is partly confounded with session number and with expectancy (p. 11).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the acute within-person comparison. For the on-haloperidol versus off-haloperidol contrast there is no randomization of medication status and the two series were separated by weeks, so time, repeated exposure to ketamine and clinical state all differ with it; baseline BPRS total was higher off haloperidol (38.3) than on it (34.6) in the placebo condition (Table 2, p. 13; Table 4, p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate comparison group). The paper compares its findings narratively with a published study of ketamine in people without schizophrenia (Krystal et al., 1994), whose infusion method differed (p. 16).

outcomes.instruments: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS; Overall and Gorham 1962), a clinician-rated scale of psychiatric symptoms, scored as the total and as five subscales: psychosis (items 4, 12 and 15), withdrawal (items 3, 13 and 16), activation (items 6, 7 and 17), anxiety (items 1, 2, 5 and 9) and hostility (items 10, 11 and 14); and the global items of the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS; Andreasen 1982), a clinician-rated scale of negative symptoms, which the paper calls the Assessment of Negative Symptoms Scale (pp. 11-12). Ratings were taken just before injection and 20, 90 and 180 minutes after it, from a clinical interview that summed everything since the previous rating. A blind follow-up interview at 8 and 24 hours after injection reviewed the experience (p. 12).
outcomes.validity_norms: Both are standard clinician-rated scales; no inter-rater reliability, no norms and no minimally important difference are reported. All ratings were made by a single research clinician, blind to drug and dose, with sessions audiotaped and clinical notes taken (p. 12).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Worsening of mental status' is a rise in BPRS total or subscale score 20 minutes after injection relative to the placebo condition. The per-person statements ('at least a 50% increase in psychosis') are proportional changes in the psychosis subscale whose individual values are not printed (p. 12). Delayed effects were not operationalized at all: they were recorded from spontaneous report at the 8- and 24-hour interviews, and the paper says they were not systematically rated because they had not been anticipated (p. 13).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The analysis was a multivariate repeated-measures analysis of variance with dose as the repeated factor, run at each time point, with planned orthogonal contrasts of each of the three doses against placebo, done separately on and off haloperidol (p. 12). Editors' count: for the four tabulated BPRS measures this is 4 measures x 3 doses x 4 time points x 2 medication conditions = 96 planned contrasts, of which about ten p-values are printed. The activation and hostility subscales and the SANS global items were measured but never tabulated.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Ratings were made blind by a single research clinician, including the 8- and 24-hour follow-up interview; one physician and one research nurse were not blind but are stated to have taken no part in the clinical assessments (pp. 11-12). No check of whether the blind held is reported, and the two safety-driven placebo substitutions for the top dose were decided by the non-blind observer, described as keeping the blind (p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported: the paper prints means with standard deviations and a small number of p-values, with no test statistics, degrees of freedom, confidence intervals or effect sizes. On haloperidol, BPRS total at 20 minutes was 33.4 (SD 6.0) after placebo, 38.3 (7.1) at 0.1 mg/kg, 39.3 (5.0) at 0.3 mg/kg (p = .005) and 45.3 (7.7) at 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01); the psychosis subscale was 8.0 (3.1), 9.8 (3.3) (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) and 12.3 (2.5) (p = .02) (Table 2, p. 13; text, p. 12). Editors' calculation from Table 2 (Cohen's d from the printed means and SDs, placebo as comparator at 20 minutes, n = 9 and n = 7): BPRS total d about 0.75 (0.1 mg/kg), 1.07 (0.3) and 1.72 (0.5); psychosis subscale d about 0.56, 0.44 and 1.53. These ignore the within-person pairing, which is what the paper tested, so they are approximate. Off haloperidol, BPRS total at 20 minutes rose from 37.3 (7.5) after placebo to 46.6 (5.9) at 0.5 mg/kg, reported only as a trend (p = 0.07, n = 5), and no psychosis-subscale increase reached significance at any dose (Table 4, p. 15; text, p. 13).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted within-person contrasts; no modelling of session order or period, although order was chosen rather than randomized.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned; the paper predates trial registration. The institutional review board reviewed the protocol during its conduct, especially as the mental-status consequences became apparent (p. 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: The SANS global items, the BPRS activation subscale and the BPRS hostility subscale were all measured (pp. 11-12) and none is reported as data: the statement that ketamine did not alter negative symptoms is referred to Table 2 (p. 12), which contains no negative-symptom measure. Only about ten p-values are printed across 96 implied contrasts, and two marked significances in the tables (the psychosis subscale at 180 minutes at 0.1 mg/kg, Table 2; the withdrawal subscale at 180 minutes at 0.5 mg/kg, Table 4) are not discussed in the text. The delayed effects, which the abstract features, were gathered by clinical report rather than rated.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With nine participants (seven at the top dose) on haloperidol and six (five at the top dose) off it, the off-haloperidol null result and the non-significant on-versus-off comparison are uninformative about the size of any difference; the authors say the lack of significant worsening off haloperidol may be due to the smaller sample, a higher baseline level of psychosis or a ceiling effect (p. 16).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nine people with schizophrenia stabilized on haloperidol, a single intravenous bolus of ketamine raised BPRS total scores 20 minutes later relative to a blinded placebo injection in the same people (0.3 mg/kg p = .005; 0.5 mg/kg p = .01), with the rise carried by the three positive-symptom items; scores were back at baseline by 90 and 180 minutes. The symptoms described at 0.1 mg/kg were perceptual distortions, illusions and depersonalization, and at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg suspiciousness, delusions, hallucinations and thought disorder, often resembling the person's own illness. In the six people retested without haloperidol, only a trend was seen at the top dose and no psychosis-subscale increase was significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title asserts that subanesthetic doses stimulate psychosis in schizophrenia, which the within-person placebo-controlled comparison supports for the acute effect on haloperidol. Three gaps. (1) The abstract calls the worsening 'short (< 30 minutes)' while ratings were taken only at 20, 90 and 180 minutes, so nothing was measured between 20 and 90 minutes; the same abstract reports delayed psychotomimetic effects at 8-24 hours, which the Table 3 heading gives as 4-24 hours and the text as about 6 to 8 hours, from spontaneous report in four of nine people. (2) The statement that ketamine failed to alter negative symptoms (p. 12) cites Table 2, which holds no negative-symptom measure; the SANS data are never shown, and the two people with the deficit syndrome went in opposite directions (one 50% worse, one 60% better, p. 12). (3) The conclusion that haloperidol failed to block the psychosis-inducing action of ketamine (p. 17) rests on a non-significant trend in five to six people and on a non-significant difference between conditions; the abstract's wording, that the results failed to indicate that haloperidol blocks the effect, is the accurate form of the same statement.

timeline.event: Krystal et al. gave ketamine by 40-minute infusion to people without schizophrenia: dose-dependent perceptual alterations, thought disorder and suspiciousness, with an increase in negative symptoms and, as this paper's discussion states, no hallucinations (p. 16)
This study: the first report of ketamine given to people with schizophrenia (the authors state the effects had not been described before, p. 10)
Lahti et al. compared ketamine in people with schizophrenia and in volunteers without it (Neuropsychopharmacology; Tier B of the list, not yet appraised)
Beck et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-induced psychiatric symptoms (JAMA Network Open; on the project's list, not yet appraised)

Ait Bentaleb et al., meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging during ketamine administration in healthy volunteers, which treats the psychotomimetic effect as the basis of the ketamine model of psychosis

replication.where_it_stands: The acute symptom-provoking effect of subanesthetic ketamine is the best-replicated part of this literature, in people with and without schizophrenia, and underlies the ketamine model of psychosis used by later imaging and meta-analytic work. The specific claims of this paper that remain single-study are the comparison of the same people on and off haloperidol, the resemblance between ketamine-induced and personal illness symptoms as rated here, and the delayed recurrences at 6-24 hours, which were not systematically measured. The strength of the evidence about antipsychotic blockade is the weakest part: it rests on five to six people.

funding.funder: Supported in part by National Institute of Mental Health Grant MH CRC 40279 (Acknowledgments, p. 17).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Maryland Psychiatric Research Center, University of Maryland School of Medicine; Department of Psychology, University of Maryland Baltimore County; Department of Anesthesiology, University of Maryland School of Medicine (p. 9). Acknowledgments name a statistician who assisted and reviewed the manuscript and a staff member who collected and analysed data (p. 17). No industry sponsor is named.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized, counterbalanced, placebo-controlled crossover in people with schizophrenia, with the medication condition itself randomized (antipsychotic versus placebo) rather than sequential, with blinding integrity tested, with ratings taken densely enough to describe onset and offset (including between 20 and 90 minutes), with negative symptoms rated on a dedicated scale and reported whatever the result, and with pre-specified systematic rating of effects at 8, 24 and 48 hours; plasma ketamine and metabolite concentrations measured alongside, so that symptom scores can be related to exposure.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the dose and placebo conditions)
domains.note: The order was not randomized: the non-blind staff selected it for safety, the highest dose was routinely not given first, and eleven orders were used across the fifteen series (p. 11). Dose is therefore partly confounded with session number, familiarity and expectancy, and no allocation-concealment procedure is described.

Four sessions spread over two weeks with no stated washout rule beyond one condition per day. The paper itself reports delayed effects at 6-24 hours in four of nine people and a fall in anxiety scores across sessions with procedure familiarity (pp. 12-13, 16), yet no period or order term is modelled.

Described as double-blind with a single blind rater, but 0.3-0.5 mg/kg of ketamine produces unmistakable effects and no blinding-integrity check is reported. A physician and a nurse were unblinded (stated to take no part in ratings), and the non-blind observer substituted placebo for the top dose in two participants on safety grounds within the blinded series (p. 11).

The top dose was given to 7 of 9 on haloperidol and to 5 of 6 off it; within the six people who did both series, Figure 2 labels only 4 at 0.5 mg/kg on haloperidol and 5 off it (p. 15). Two of the three people who did not enter the off-haloperidol series declined because of their first ketamine experience, which is related to the outcome. The two who did not receive the top condition on haloperidol were withheld by the non-blind observer on safety grounds and given a blinded placebo in its place, so the missingness at the top of the range is itself related to how people were responding.

BPRS and SANS global items are standard clinician-rated instruments applied blind by one rater from an interview summing events since the last rating, but no inter-rater reliability is given, there is a single rater, and the delayed effects were captured only by spontaneous clinical report because they had not been anticipated (p. 13).

No protocol. The SANS global items, the activation subscale and the hostility subscale were measured and never reported, while the text draws a negative-symptom conclusion and cites a table that contains no negative-symptom measure (p. 12). About ten p-values are printed for roughly 96 implied dose-versus-placebo contrasts, with no test statistics or degrees of freedom anywhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person placebo comparison is the strength of the design, and the acute increases at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg are large relative to the sources of bias named (editors' calculation, d about 1.1 and 1.7 on BPRS total). The overall judgment is set by the non-randomized order chosen by unblinded staff, the absence of any blinding check in a drug whose effects are obvious, and the reporting: measured negative-symptom data are missing while a negative-symptom conclusion is drawn. The source can be cited for the acute symptom-provoking effect of a single intravenous ketamine bolus at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg in nine people with schizophrenia on haloperidol, for its 20-minute peak and return to baseline by 90 minutes, and for the clinical description of the induced symptoms in this sample. It cannot be cited for an effect or absence of effect on negative symptoms, for whether antipsychotic medication blocks the response, for the dose-response shape, or for the frequency of delayed effects.

key_findings.finding: On haloperidol, BPRS total score 20 minutes after the injection rose from 33.4 (SD 6.0) after placebo to 38.3 (7.1) at 0.1 mg/kg, 39.3 (5.0) at 0.3 mg/kg and 45.3 (7.7) at 0.5 mg/kg; the increase was significant at 0.3 mg/kg (p = .005) and 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01). Baseline (time 0) values were 34.6 (7.0), 33.2 (4.2), 35.2 (5.4) and 36.9 (11.0). n = 9 for placebo, 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg and n = 7 for 0.5 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Table 2, BPRS Total Score rows (p. 13)
key_findings.note: The paper never says whether the values in parentheses, here and in Tables 1, 2 and 4, are standard deviations or standard errors; reading them as standard deviations is the editors' reading, and is the only reading the magnitudes allow (11.0 as a standard error at n=7 would imply a standard deviation of about 29 on the BPRS). Two of the nine did not receive the 0.5 mg/kg condition on haloperidol and were given placebo blindly as a dose substitution (p. 11), so the placebo column holds, for two people, an injection given in place of the largest amount.

key_findings.finding: The rise was carried by positive symptoms: the BPRS psychosis subscale (items 4, 12 and 15) at 20 minutes was 8.0 (SD 3.1) after placebo, 9.8 (3.3) at 0.1 mg/kg (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) at 0.3 mg/kg and 12.3 (2.5) at 0.5 mg/kg (p = .02), against baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Table 2, BPRS Psychosis Subscale rows (p. 13)
key_findings.note: The 0.3 mg/kg psychosis increase is not marked significant in Table 2 and no p-value is given for it, although the total score at that dose is the paper's most significant result.

key_findings.finding: The effect was short-lived as measured: BPRS total scores were back at or below baseline at 90 and 180 minutes in every condition (for example 0.5 mg/kg: 45.3 at 20 minutes, 32.3 at 90 minutes, 32.3 at 180 minutes).
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Table 2 (p. 13)
key_findings.note: There is no measurement between 20 and 90 minutes, so the abstract's 'short (< 30 minutes)' is an inference from these two time points.

key_findings.finding: Seven of the nine participants showed at least a 50% increase in psychosis during the ketamine injections, one showed a change of less than 25% and one did not change; the person who did not change was the oldest (53) and had the longest illness (24 years).
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); patient 8 in Table 1 (p. 11)
key_findings.note: Individual psychosis scores are not printed, so the per-person percentages cannot be checked; the group means rise by 44% (0.1 mg/kg), 41% (0.3) and 78% (0.5) from their own baselines (editors' calculation from Table 2).

key_findings.finding: Symptoms by dose, as described by the raters: at 0.1 mg/kg perceptual distortions, illusions and depersonalization; at 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg suspiciousness, delusions, hallucinations (visual and auditory) and thought disorder (loose associations, incoherence, flight of ideas).
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The induced symptoms often reproduced the person's own illness: two people with extensive paranoid delusions reactivated part of those specific delusions, and some people who had no thought disorder on haloperidol became disorganized in ways characteristic of their untreated illness. Table 3 sets each participant's usual symptoms beside the symptoms seen 20 minutes after ketamine.

Anxiety did not track ketamine: no significant increase in the BPRS anxiety subscale at any dose or time except 0.3 mg/kg at 180 minutes, and anxiety scores tended to fall across the 180 minutes within each dose level. The authors read the anxiety as anticipatory and falling with familiarity with the procedure.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 3rd paragraph (p. 12); Table 2, BPRS Anxiety Subscale rows (p. 13); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Four of the nine participants spontaneously reported a delayed return of psychotic symptoms at the 8- and 24-hour interviews: two had ketamine-induced delusions recur about 6 to 8 hours afterwards, lasting several hours but not severe and needing no treatment, one reported active dreaming the following night, and one reported the same visual hallucinations recurring occasionally over the next several days and refused the second series because of it. All were asymptomatic at 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 4th (last) paragraph (p. 12) continuing on p. 13
key_findings.note: The paper states these data are descriptive, gathered by clinical report and not systematically rated, because delayed effects had not been anticipated (p. 13). The 8- and 24-hour interviews were themselves conducted blind to the condition, by the same clinician who made the session ratings (p. 11), which is a little stronger than an unstructured clinical report.

key_findings.finding: Off haloperidol (six people retested), the BPRS total at 20 minutes rose from 37.3 (SD 7.5) after placebo to 38.5 (5.6), 44.7 (7.4) and 46.6 (5.9) at 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, with only a trend at the top dose (p = 0.07, n = 5); no psychosis-subscale increase was significant at any dose. The BPRS withdrawal subscale was significantly raised at 180 minutes at 0.5 mg/kg (p < .05, n = 5).
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Neuroleptic-Free Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 13); Table 4 (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: In the six people who completed both series, neither the increase in BPRS total and psychosis scores at 20 minutes nor the baseline psychosis score differed significantly between the on- and off-haloperidol conditions; on haloperidol these same six showed only a trend at the top dose (p < .1). All six were more symptomatic during the neuroleptic-free period, but that difference was not significant either.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Neuroleptic-Free Subjects, 2nd paragraph (p. 13) continuing on p. 14; Figure 2 (p. 15)
key_findings.note: Figure 2's own labels show that at 0.5 mg/kg only 4 of these 6 were tested on haloperidol and 5 off it, so the comparison at the top dose rests on at most four paired observations.

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms did not change overall, as the paper reports it; of the two participants who met criteria for the deficit syndrome, one had negative symptoms worsen by 50% and the other improve by 60%, while positive symptoms increased in both. In the first 3 to 5 minutes after injection participants typically appeared withdrawn and without spontaneous communication but, the paper states, were always responsive, and later described active mental events during that time; the withdrawal subscale rose slightly from each condition's own baseline at the 20-minute rating (7.1 to 7.6 after placebo, 8.2 to 8.9, 8.0 to 8.8 and 7.3 to 8.6 after the three amounts) with none of the rises marked significant.
key_findings.locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 2nd paragraph (p. 12); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 16)
key_findings.note: Measured negative-symptom data (SANS global items) are never reported; the statement is referred to Table 2, which contains the BPRS total and the psychosis, withdrawal and anxiety subscales only.

key_findings.finding: Design facts that bound every result: four intravenous conditions (placebo and 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 mg/kg) given over 60 seconds, one per day across two weeks; order chosen by non-blind staff for safety with the highest dose routinely not given first, eleven different orders across the fifteen series; ratings at baseline and 20, 90 and 180 minutes by one blind clinician; haloperidol 0.3 mg/kg/day for four weeks before the first series.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Experimental Overview and Ketamine Administration Procedure (p. 11); Mental Status Evaluation and Data Analysis (pp. 11-12)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 prints the BPRS psychosis subscale at 180 minutes for the 0.5 mg/kg condition as 38.2 (4.3), which is the BPRS total-score value in the same cell position of the same table; a three-item subscale whose other values run from 9.8 to 12.4 cannot take that value.
reporting_issues.consequence: A transcription error in the published table. The off-haloperidol psychosis time course cannot be read as printed at that one cell; nothing in the text depends on it, but the number must never be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that visual hallucinations were frequent in all the patients (p. 13), while Table 3, which lists each participant's acute drug effects, records visual hallucinations for five of the nine; participant 8 is listed as 'No change' and participant 9 as auditory hallucinations only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prose generalizes beyond the per-person table. Any claim about how commonly ketamine produced visual hallucinations in this sample should use Table 3, not the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Two marked significances in the tables are never mentioned in the text: the psychosis subscale at 180 minutes at 0.1 mg/kg (7.0, marked p < .05 against placebo 7.9) in Table 2, and the withdrawal subscale at 180 minutes at 0.5 mg/kg (11.0, marked p < .05) in Table 4; conversely, the 0.3 mg/kg psychosis increase at 20 minutes carries no mark and no p-value although the text treats the psychosis subscale as the carrier of the total-score change.
reporting_issues.consequence: The set of significant results in the tables and the set discussed in the text do not match, so the reader cannot tell which contrasts were planned and which are incidental; with about 96 implied contrasts and no correction, isolated marks at 180 minutes are of no evidential value.

reporting_issues.issue: The duration of the delayed effects is given three different ways: the abstract says 8-24 hours, the heading of Table 3 says 4-24 hr, and the text says the delusions recurred about 6 to 8 hours after ketamine, with one person reporting recurrences over several days.
reporting_issues.consequence: No single window can be quoted for the delayed effects; the underlying observations were spontaneous reports from four of nine people, not measurements, and the card states them as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that ketamine failed to alter negative mental symptoms cites Table 2 (p. 12), but Table 2 reports only the BPRS total and its psychosis, withdrawal and anxiety subscales. The SANS global items named in the Methods as the negative-symptom measure are never reported, and the BPRS activation and hostility subscales, discussed in the text as showing no change, are not tabulated either.
reporting_issues.consequence: The negative-symptom conclusion of this paper is unsupported by any shown data and must not be cited; the discussion builds on it to contrast people with schizophrenia against the volunteers of Krystal et al. (1994), so that comparison is weakened too.

reporting_issues.issue: No test statistics, degrees of freedom, confidence intervals or effect sizes are given anywhere; the results are means with standard deviations and about ten bare p-values, some printed in the text and some only as table footnote marks.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nothing can be re-checked or pooled from the printed statistics; effect sizes for the encyclopedia have to be computed from the tabulated means and SDs, which ignores the within-person pairing the paper tested and so is approximate (and is labelled as the editors' calculation on this card).

reporting_issues.issue: The number of people contributing to the top dose differs between places: Table 2 gives n = 7 on haloperidol and Table 4 n = 5 off it, while Figure 2, which compares the six people who did both series, labels n = 4 at 0.5 mg/kg on haloperidol and n = 5 off it. The text says three subjects failed to receive the highest dose without saying in which series.
reporting_issues.consequence: The central comparison of the paper, ketamine on versus off haloperidol at the top dose, rests on at most four paired observations; the text's null result should be read with that number, which only the figure labels disclose.

reporting_issues.issue: Dose units slip in the text: the off-haloperidol result is given for 'the 0.5-mg ketamine dose' and 'the 0.5-mg dose' (p. 13), and the case vignettes describe 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg (p. 14), where the Methods and tables give mg/kg.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical, but a reader quoting the text would report a fixed milligram dose for a weight-based one; the encyclopedia uses the mg/kg values of the Methods and tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is cited in the text for the total BPRS score ('Ketamine increased total BPRS score ... (Figure 1 and Table 2)', p. 12), but its y-axis is the BPRS psychosis score and its plotted values (about 8 to 12.3) match the psychosis subscale of Table 2, not the total (31 to 45).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure shows a different outcome from the one the sentence citing it reports; anchors for the total score should cite Table 2, and anchors for the psychosis time course Figure 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Baseline BPRS totals in the placebo condition differ between the two series (34.6 on haloperidol, 38.3 off it) and the paper reports that all participants were more symptomatic while neuroleptic-free, yet the on- versus off-haloperidol comparison of ketamine-induced change is made without adjusting for baseline or modelling the ceiling the authors themselves invoke.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison that supports the paper's statement about haloperidol is confounded by different starting scores in the same people, as the discussion concedes; the card treats it as uninformative rather than as evidence of no blockade.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Lahti_1995_KetaminePsychosisSchizophrenia.pdf, printed pp. 9-19 in full (text, Tables 1-4, Figures 1 and 2 with their labels, case vignettes, acknowledgments and reference list). The PDF is a scan with machine-read text that misspells names and units, so every number on this card was read from the rendered page images at 150 and 300 dpi rather than from the text extraction.

disagreements.first_pass: no note; the parenthesised values were labelled SD without qualification
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 225 (corrected): the paper never says whether the values in parentheses are SD or SEM, so the 'SD' label should be marked as the editors' reading; (missed) the two people who did not receive the largest amount on haloperidol were given a blinded placebo as a dose substitution
disagreements.resolution: Both accepted after reading Table 2 and p. 11 rendered at 150 dpi: no table or text labels the dispersion, and the placebo substitution is stated in the Methods. The numbers are unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: participants typically appeared withdrawn and unresponsive in manner … at the 20-minute rating they reported no increase in withdrawal symptoms
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 225: 'no increase in withdrawal symptoms' is better put as no significant change, because the withdrawal subscale did rise slightly from each condition's own baseline at 20 minutes
disagreements.resolution: Accepted, and a second error corrected on my own reading of the rendered p. 12: the paper says participants appeared withdrawn 'without spontaneous communication, but were always responsive', so 'unresponsive in manner' reversed the source. The Table 2 withdrawal values are now given.

disagreements.first_pass: described the delayed reports only as descriptive clinical report
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 225 (missed): the follow-up interviews at 8 and 24 hours were conducted blind to drug and dose by the same clinician, which strengthens the delayed-report observations a little
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 11: the Mental Status Evaluation paragraph states that the follow-up interview at 8 and 24 hours was again conducted blind to the drug or dose by the same clinician.

disagreements.first_pass: three did not receive the 0.5 mg/kg dose in it (Table 2 gives n=7)
disagreements.resolution: Corrected: 9 minus 3 is 6, but Table 2 prints n=7 for that condition on haloperidol and Table 4 prints n=5 of 6 off it, so two were missing in the on-haloperidol series and one in the off-haloperidol series; the paper's 'overall, three subjects failed to receive the highest ketamine dose' (p. 11) counts both series.

disagreements.first_pass: did not say why the top-condition data were missing
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 225: would add to the missing-data domain that two of the nine were placebo-substituted at the largest amount, so the missingness at the top of the dose range is related to how people responded
disagreements.resolution: Accepted as a factual addition; the judgment (some-concerns) and the overall judgment (high) are unchanged, and both readers agree on the overall rating.
